Today I want to look at a farming system that is, in some ways, older and simpler than irrigation: flood-recession agriculture. Picture a river that floods every year at roughly the same time. When the water rises, it spreads over the low land on either side and leaves behind a layer of fine, nutrient-rich silt. Then, as the flood recedes, farmers plant seeds directly into the damp soil. The crop grows on moisture stored in the ground, so there's no need to dig channels or lift water. Now, you might think this sounds almost too easy, and in a good year, it was. The silt replaced nutrients every season, so fields could be farmed for centuries without wearing out. Compare that with rain-fed fields elsewhere, which often had to be left empty for years to recover. But the system had a serious weakness. It depended entirely on the size of the flood. If the river rose too little, the upper fields stayed dry and couldn't be planted. If it rose too much, the water stayed on the land too long, and planting came too late in the season. So farmers became very interested in predicting the flood. Some communities kept records of water levels, marking them on stone, and over generations those records became a kind of early science. In fact, some historians argue that it was the need to manage uncertainty, rather than the need to grow more food, that pushed these societies toward more complex forms of administration.

Let's talk about an idea from public health that many people find counterintuitive. It's called the prevention paradox. Suppose a city wants to reduce heart disease. The obvious strategy is to find the small group of people at very high risk, say, those with extremely high blood pressure, and treat them. That certainly helps those individuals. But here's the thing: most heart attacks in that city won't happen to the high-risk group. They'll happen to the much larger group of people at moderate risk, simply because there are so many more of them. So an alternative strategy is to shift the whole population a little, for instance, by reducing the salt in processed foods. Each person's blood pressure drops only slightly, and any one individual benefits very little. Yet across hundreds of thousands of people, the number of heart attacks prevented can be larger than with the targeted approach. That's the paradox: a measure that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each person who takes part. And this creates a practical problem. If you ask people to change their behavior for a benefit they'll never personally notice, many won't bother. That's why population strategies tend to work best when they don't depend on individual effort at all, when the change happens in the food supply or the environment rather than through personal choices.

Today we'll talk about how babies learn to speak. Babies don't say real words at first. At about six months old, they start to babble. Babbling means making the same simple sounds again and again, like ba-ba-ba or da-da-da. Babies all over the world babble in a similar way. But by around ten months, something changes. Their babbling starts to sound more like the language they hear at home. A baby in a Spanish-speaking family begins to sound a little Spanish, and a baby in a Japanese-speaking family begins to sound a little Japanese. Most babies say their first real word around their first birthday. Parents can help by talking to their babies often, even before the babies understand.

Astronomers have found thousands of planets around other stars. But which ones might have life? One important idea is the habitable zone. This is the area around a star where a planet is not too hot and not too cold, so water can stay liquid. If a planet is too close to its star, the water boils away. If it is too far, the water freezes. Earth is in the habitable zone of our Sun. Being in this zone does not mean that a planet has life. It only means that liquid water is possible. Scientists then use powerful telescopes to study the planet's air for other clues.

Hi everyone, a quick announcement on behalf of the Child Language Lab. The lab is recruiting families with children between eighteen and thirty months old for a study on how toddlers learn new verbs. Sessions take about forty minutes. The child watches short videos while an eye tracker records where they look. Parents receive a twenty-dollar gift card, and the child gets to pick a book to take home. I should mention that, because the study looks at early vocabulary, the lab can only include children who hear mainly English at home. A separate study for bilingual families will run in the spring. The sign-up link is on the department page.

I want to pick up a point from last week about infants and speech sounds. Every language uses a limited set of contrasts, that is, differences between sounds that change the meaning of a word. English distinguishes r and l, so rock and lock are different words. Japanese doesn't make that distinction. What's remarkable is that infants around six months old can hear differences between sounds from virtually any language, including contrasts their parents can't hear at all. But by about their first birthday, that ability has narrowed. Babies become better at the contrasts in their own language and noticeably worse at the ones they don't hear around them. Researchers call this perceptual narrowing. At first glance, it looks like a loss. Why would the brain throw away a useful ability? But think about what the infant is doing. It's learning which differences matter. If you treated every tiny variation as meaningful, you'd struggle to recognize that two people saying the same word are, in fact, saying the same word. So narrowing is better understood as tuning than as decline. One more thing: exposure seems to have to be social. In one line of research, infants who heard a new language from a live speaker kept the ability to hear its contrasts, but infants who heard the same speech from a video recording did not.

Let's turn to early wheat. Wild wheat has a feature that's great for the plant but terrible for a farmer: when the seeds ripen, the head of the plant shatters, and the seeds fall to the ground on their own. That's how the plant spreads. Domesticated wheat, by contrast, keeps its seeds on the stalk until someone harvests them. So at some point, people must have selected plants that didn't shatter. For a long time, researchers assumed this happened quickly. Experiments with modern wild wheat suggested that if farmers harvested with sickles, non-shattering plants would dominate a field within twenty or thirty years. But the archaeological record tells a different story. Preserved plant remains from early sites show that non-shattering wheat took something like two thousand years to become dominant. So why the gap? One explanation is harvesting technique. If people gathered wheat before it was fully ripe, or simply pulled up whole plants, they'd collect shattering and non-shattering seeds alike, and there'd be little pressure favoring one type over the other. In other words, the speed of domestication may have depended less on the plant than on human habits.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Finding Planets Around Other Stars

For most of history, astronomers could only speculate about whether other stars had planets. The difficulty is one of contrast: a planet is billions of times fainter than the star it orbits, and from Earth the two appear almost on top of each other. Since the 1990s, however, more than five thousand such worlds, called exoplanets, have been confirmed, most of them without ever being seen directly.

The most productive technique is the transit method. When a planet passes between its star and an observer, it blocks a tiny fraction of the star's light. A telescope that measures the star's brightness continuously will record a small, regular dip each time this happens. The depth of the dip reveals the planet's size relative to the star, and the time between dips gives the length of its year.

The method has an important bias. A transit can be observed only if the planet's orbit is lined up almost exactly with our line of sight, so most planetary systems are invisible to it. Moreover, planets that orbit close to their stars transit frequently and are detected quickly, whereas a planet with an orbit as long as Jupiter's might pass in front of its star only once every twelve years.

Long ago, people did not keep animals on farms. They hunted wild animals for food. About ten thousand years ago, people in the Middle East began to keep wild goats near their homes. Over time, these goats became calmer and smaller. People used them for milk, meat and skin. Goats were very useful because they can eat many plants that people cannot eat. Later, people also kept sheep, cows and pigs. Keeping animals meant that families had food all year, even in winter.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Statistical Learning in Infancy

Spoken language poses a problem that written language does not: there are no reliable pauses between words. A listener who does not yet know a language's vocabulary therefore faces a continuous stream of sound, and it was long assumed that infants must rely on innate knowledge to divide it into words. A series of experiments beginning in the 1990s complicated that assumption. Eight-month-old infants listened for two minutes to an artificial 'language' of nonsense syllables strung together without pauses or stress. Within the stream, certain syllables always followed one another, forming 'words', while other pairings occurred only by chance, at word boundaries. When later presented with sequences from the stream, the infants listened longer to the chance pairings, indicating that they had registered which syllables reliably belonged together.

The finding was striking less for its demonstration of learning than for the speed and the kind of computation involved: the infants were, in effect, tracking transitional probabilities, the likelihood that one sound predicts the next. Yet researchers have been cautious about its scope. Natural speech is far richer and noisier than an artificial stream, and the ability to detect patterns does not by itself explain how infants attach meaning to the units they discover. Statistical learning is thus better described as one tool among several than as a complete account of how language is acquired.

email.title: Write an Email
email.to: Ms. Alvarez, Director of Campus Dining
email.subject: Dining hall hours
email.prompt:
You live in a residence hall and have a meal plan. This semester, the main dining hall changed its weekday closing time from 9:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. You have a chemistry lab that ends at 7:15 p.m. three evenings a week.

Write an email to Ms. Alvarez, the director of Campus Dining. In your email, do the following:
- Explain your situation.
- Describe how the new hours affect you.
- Suggest a solution that would help students like you.

Use full sentences, and write as much as you can.
email.rubric: Task: email to a university administrator about a service problem. Must cover all 3 bullets: the situation (lab ends 7:15, dining closes 7:00), a concrete effect (missed dinners, paying twice, eating poorly), and a specific, realistic solution (late window, take-out box, later hours on lab days). Look for polite, formal-neutral register, greeting and sign-off, logical organization, accurate and varied grammar, precise word choice. Typical strong length 100-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on linguistics. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, do these two things:
- State your view and back it up.
- Add something new to the thread, in your own words.

Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Mensah
professor.text: Many countries now introduce a second language in the first year of primary school, at age six or even earlier. Supporters say young children learn languages more naturally. Others argue that the money would be better spent on teaching a second language intensively to older students, who learn grammar faster and can study more independently. If you were advising a school system, which approach would you recommend, and why?

students.name: Lena
students.text: I'd start early. Young children aren't embarrassed to make mistakes, and they pick up pronunciation in a way teenagers rarely do. Even an hour a week builds familiarity, so the language never feels foreign later on.

students.name: Omar
students.text: I'm not convinced. In my primary school, the language teacher visited once a week and we mostly sang songs. By the time we were twelve, we had to start again from the beginning. Intensive classes for older students would have been far more useful.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear position on early versus later language instruction, specific reasons or examples, engagement with Lena's or Omar's point (agreeing with extension, or rebutting, not repeating), coherence, and varied, accurate grammar and vocabulary.
